title: Zippers: Humans’ Greatest Invention? No, But Still Good
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the zipper, starting with buttons and button-making guilds, then Elias Howe Jr.'s 1851 automatic continuous clothing closure patent, Whitcomb Judson's Universal Fastener Company and Judson Security Fastener shown at the Chicago World's Fair, and Gideon Sundback's hookless fasteners that became the modern zipper. They cover early uses (military money belts, pilot flight suits, B.F. Goodrich galoshes called "zippers"), fashion resistance to zippers, zippers in jeans, the three zipper types, YKK's rise to dominance, how a zipper mechanically works, zipper repair tips, zipper injuries, and a listener mail message about healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.
topics: Levi's zipper fly vs button fly

segments.title: Opening banter and room spray
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about room spray, lotion, and a friend's new baby, then set up the episode topic of zippers and buttons.

segments.title: Buttons and early fasteners
segments.summary: The hosts trace buttons from a shell button in the Indus Valley around five thousand years ago through loop-and-bone fasteners, the 1250 French button makers guild, and the invention of the buttonhole.

segments.title: Elias Howe's 1851 patent and Whitcomb Judson
segments.summary: Elias Howe Jr. patented an automatic continuous clothing closure in 1851, a predecessor of the zipper, which he did not pursue. About forty-four years later, Whitcomb Judson of Chicago marketed a clasp fastener for shoes with Colonel Lewis Walker, forming the Universal Fastener Company.

segments.title: Judson Security Fastener at the World's Fair
segments.summary: The Judson Security Fastener debuted at the Chicago World's Fair but flopped because it was unreliable and expensive, and it was still a clasp-and-hook design rather than a true zipper. Judson then hired Gideon Sundback.

segments.title: Gideon Sundback and the hookless fastener
segments.summary: Swedish-born electrical engineer Gideon Sundback improved the design with teeth instead of clasps, about ten or eleven per inch, and built a machine to produce them. His hookless number two became the modern zipper, and the company was renamed Hookless Fastener Company.

segments.title: Early zipper uses: military, boots, and galoshes
segments.summary: The US Army ordered zippers for sailors' money belts and pilot flight suits. B.F. Goodrich galoshes with zippers gave the name 'zipper' to the boots before the term applied to the fastener itself.

segments.title: Zippers in fashion, jeans, and the button fly debate
segments.summary: Zippers were slow to catch on in fashion, partly because they were seen as improper for women. Designers Elsa Schiaparelli and Edward Molyneux used them in the 1930s, children's clothing promoted them, and Levi's added zippers to jeans in the mid-1940s for Eastern women. The hosts discuss the button fly versus zipper fly debate, citing Esquire.

segments.title: Zipper types, production growth, and YKK
segments.summary: The hosts describe closed-end, open-end, and two-way zippers, and production growth from 24,000 zippers in 1917 to 60 million in 1934 and 2.3 billion by 1971. YKK, founded in 1934 and making about five million zippers a day, overtook Talon's market share around 1970.

segments.title: How a zipper works, repair tips, and special zippers
segments.summary: Josh explains the slide body, bridge, and puller, and how the offset teeth interlock through wedges in the slide. He covers repair tips such as clamping a loose slide with pliers and unsticking zippers with graphite, bar soap, or Windex. He also mentions locking and magnetic zippers and how zippers are made from metal, plastic, and woven nylon coil.

segments.title: Zipper injuries
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2013 San Francisco urology study of about 18,000 zipper injuries in emergency rooms, with the treatment of pouring mineral oil on the injury. They note that toilet lids caused more penile injuries than zippers.

segments.title: Listener mail from Kirsten and Matt
segments.summary: A listener named Kirsten writes that the show helps her and her boyfriend Matt, an ICU worker, during the coronavirus pandemic. The hosts thank healthcare workers.
